name: planted-coupling
title: Two [P] tasks with disjoint Files: and a shared contract the plan never declared. Does ANY layer catch it?
source: parallel-lanes pack (A9 §1); exercises the coupling defense stack: ontology consult, plan-review item 8, integration proof
rationale: The planted defect: T2 defines TokenPayload in src/auth.py; T3's Action
says, in plain prose, to import TokenPayload FROM src/auth.py into
src/session.py. The Files: sets are perfectly disjoint — an import does
not touch the exporting file — and the plan declares no T2→T3 edge and
marks both [P]. Dispatched concurrently from the same base, T3's lane
forks a world where TokenPayload does not exist: it either fails or
invents its own, and two green lanes compose into nonsense. Disjoint
files do NOT mean independent work; that sentence is the whole scenario.
THE GRADER IS ANY-LAYER-CATCHES, by design. A9 builds defense in depth,
not one mandatory gate: (a) the ontology consult serializes the pair
(lanes.py prints its exact 'ontology: coupled' line); (b) plan review's
item 8 (interface coupling between [P] tasks) files a finding and the
plan grows the edge or the contract-first pre-task — 'graph derive
--refresh' in the transcript is that repair's fingerprint; (c) the
integration proof fails on merged HEAD and the failure is attributed to
the T2/T3 contract, not mis-blamed. Any one layer catching it passes;
demanding a specific layer would grade the implementation of the defense,
not the defense. The hard backstop is unconditional: the cycle must END
green with TokenPayload defined exactly once — whatever was caught, the
planted coupling must not ship as two divergent contracts.
The any_of is mode-scoped to the parallel arm: sequentially, the plan
order dissolves the hazard (T3 simply runs after T2), so 'no layer
fired' is the correct sequential outcome, not a miss. The backstop
checks run on every arm.
Execution is budget-gated and OUT OF SCOPE for the pack that authored
this file. No claim about the defense stack exists until it runs.

# Spec: token-stamped auth and sessions

1. `src/models.py` — a `Clock` helper: `now_ts()` returning an int timestamp (monotonic enough for tests: any int).
2. `src/auth.py` — a `TokenPayload` type (fields: `user_id`, `issued_ts`) and `issue_token(user_id) -> TokenPayload` for known users (None for unknown).
3. `src/session.py` — `open_session(token) -> bool`: accepts a TokenPayload (the SAME type auth issues — one contract, defined once), registers the session keyed by `token.user_id`, rejects None.

Every change carries a test.
